weeks.title: The Math Behind the Models — Statistics, Probability, and Linear Algebra
weeks.context: Most ML failures are statistical failures dressed up as engineering ones. This week you anchor the math — distributions, expectation, variance, central limit, Bayes, eigenvectors — to the actual things you'll see in train loops and eval reports. If you skip this week you'll spend 23 weeks pattern-matching without understanding.
topics: Distributions you actually meet — Normal, Bernoulli, Categorical, Beta, Poisson
Sampling and the Central Limit Theorem — why averaging fixes things
Bias and variance — bias-variance decomposition, why both matter
Probability vs likelihood — the deepest source of beginner confusion
Bayes rule — prior, likelihood, posterior, why ML is mostly applied Bayes
Linear algebra essentials — matrix-vector multiplication as composition of linear maps
Eigenvectors and eigenvalues — what PCA is actually doing
Information theory primer — entropy, cross-entropy, KL divergence
tasks: Generate samples from 5 distributions in NumPy; plot histograms; verify mean and variance match the analytical values
Implement the bias-variance decomposition on a simple problem (e.g. polynomial regression of degree 1-15 on a noisy sine wave); plot bias², variance, total error
Implement PCA from scratch using SVD; apply to MNIST 784-dim vectors; reconstruct images from top-50 components
Implement cross-entropy loss in NumPy; verify against PyTorch's nn.CrossEntropyLoss on 10 random inputs
Pick a simple Bayesian problem (the disease-test problem) and compute the posterior by hand AND in code; convince yourself the answer is right
weeks.project: Build a Statistical EDA tool. Given any CSV, produce: per-column distribution plot (with best-fit reference distribution), correlation heatmap, mutual information matrix, missing-data pattern visualisation, outlier detection (IQR + isolation forest), and a 1-page automated report. Use SciPy for the statistics, Plotly for interactivity. Run it on 3 different real datasets. This becomes your first move on every new ML problem.

weeks.title: scikit-learn — The Library That Started It All
weeks.context: Before PyTorch, before deep learning, there was scikit-learn. It's still the right tool for 80% of tabular problems. This week you learn its API deeply — Pipeline, ColumnTransformer, cross_val_score, GridSearchCV — because once you know it, every ML library makes sense.
topics: The estimator API — .fit(), .predict(), .transform(), why every model looks the same
Pipeline and ColumnTransformer — composing preprocessing + model in one object
Train/validation/test splits — why three, when one is enough
Cross-validation — k-fold, stratified, time-series-split, group k-fold
Hyperparameter search — GridSearchCV, RandomizedSearchCV, Optuna
Categorical encoding — OneHot, Target, Ordinal, when each is right
Imputation strategies — mean, median, mode, KNN, iterative
Class imbalance — class_weight, SMOTE, when to bother
tasks: Build a Pipeline for the Titanic dataset: ColumnTransformer (numeric standardise, categorical one-hot, missing imputation) + a model. Fit, evaluate on test.
Run 5-fold cross-validation on three model families (Logistic Regression, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting). Report mean and std of accuracy.
Run hyperparameter search with both GridSearchCV and Optuna; compare time-to-best-score
Take a tabular dataset and try 5 different categorical encoding strategies; report effect on a downstream model
Implement learning curves: plot training and validation score as a function of training set size
weeks.project: Build a Tabular Benchmark. Given any CSV with a target column, your tool: detects column types, builds an appropriate preprocessing pipeline, runs 5 model families (Logistic/Linear Regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost) with default + tuned hyperparameters, produces a leaderboard with metrics, time to fit, time to predict. Test on 3 different datasets — Titanic, California Housing, Adult Income. This is the rapid-prototyping tool you'll reuse forever.

weeks.title: Feature Engineering — Where Models Are Won or Lost
weeks.context: A well-engineered feature beats a fancier model 80% of the time. This week you learn the canonical feature-engineering patterns — interactions, encodings, time features, target encoding done safely — and you learn how to build a Feature Store-like discipline even if you never use a real Feature Store.
topics: Numeric transformations — log, Box-Cox, Yeo-Johnson, when each helps
Interaction features — multiplicative, polynomial, why most are ignored by tree models
Time features — hour-of-day, day-of-week, time-since-event, lagged features
Target encoding — the right way (k-fold), the wrong way (leakage city)
Frequency and count encoding for high-cardinality categoricals
Aggregation features — group statistics from history
Text features for tabular pipelines — TF-IDF, sentence embeddings as features
Feature selection — filter, wrapper, embedded; when to bother
tasks: Take the Bike Sharing dataset and build at least 15 engineered features (time features, lags, rolling stats, interactions); measure lift
Implement k-fold target encoding from scratch; verify zero leakage by checking that out-of-fold predictions never use their own target
Use feature importance from a tree model to drop the bottom 50% of features; verify the score doesn't degrade
Build a Pipeline that includes a custom transformer that adds time features; integrate it into a model
On a high-cardinality categorical (say, a column with 10000+ unique values) try frequency, target, and embedding encodings; compare downstream metric
weeks.project: Build a Feature Store Lite. A small library where each feature is a typed Python function with a name, version, and decorator that registers it. Given a dataframe and a list of feature names, your tool computes them in order, caching intermediate dataframes to disk (Parquet). Track lineage — which features depend on which. Versioning — feature v2 doesn't overwrite v1. Test on the Bike Sharing dataset with 20 features; show that adding a new feature doesn't trigger recomputation of unchanged features.

weeks.title: Linear and Logistic Regression — Truly Understanding the Workhorse
weeks.context: Linear and logistic regression are still in production at every Fortune 500. They're interpretable, fast, robust, and they often beat XGBoost when the data is genuinely linear. This week you go deep on what they actually compute, when they fail, and what regularisation does to coefficients.
topics: OLS regression — closed form, gradient descent, when each is preferred
Logistic regression — likelihood, log-odds, the sigmoid as a smooth indicator
Regularisation — L1 (Lasso), L2 (Ridge), Elastic Net, what they do to coefficients
Interaction and polynomial terms — explicit feature engineering for linear models
Multi-class extensions — one-vs-rest, multinomial, softmax
Diagnostics — residual plots, leverage, Cook's distance, why they matter
Coefficient interpretation — odds ratios, partial effects, why they break with multicollinearity
When to reach for linear — sample-efficient, interpretable, fast inference, online learnable
tasks: Fit OLS on the California Housing data; interpret coefficients in original units; plot residuals to check assumptions
Fit logistic regression on a binary classification task; compute and interpret odds ratios
Compare Ridge, Lasso, Elastic Net with increasing regularisation strength; plot how coefficients shrink
Demonstrate overfitting with high-degree polynomial features; show how regularisation rescues it
Implement Stochastic Gradient Descent for logistic regression from scratch; match sklearn within 1% accuracy
weeks.project: Build a Loan Default Predictor — interpretable edition. Use the Kaggle Home Credit Default Risk dataset (or any credit dataset). Build a logistic-regression-based model with thoughtful feature engineering. Goal: ROC AUC > 0.78. Critically, your deliverable is interpretability: a report showing exactly why each prediction was made, the global feature importance, and an analysis of which sub-populations the model treats unfairly. Compare to XGBoost on the same features.

weeks.title: Trees and Ensembles — The Tabular Powerhouse
weeks.context: Decision trees by themselves are unstable. Hundreds of them, averaged or boosted, dominate every tabular ML competition. This week you understand why — bagging, boosting, gradient boosting — and you become fluent in XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost.
topics: Decision trees — splitting criteria (Gini, entropy, MSE), max depth, leaf size
Bagging — bootstrap aggregation, why it reduces variance
Random Forest — bagged trees + random feature subsampling, why both
Boosting — sequentially correcting errors, gradient boosting math
XGBoost vs LightGBM vs CatBoost — the differences that matter in practice
Hyperparameter tuning for boosting — learning rate, depth, n_estimators, regularisation
Early stopping — using a validation set to find the right n_estimators
Feature importance and partial dependence — what trees do, not just predict
tasks: Fit a Random Forest and an XGBoost on the same tabular dataset; compare metrics, training time, prediction time
Hand-implement a depth-2 decision tree on a toy dataset; verify your splits match what sklearn would find
Run hyperparameter search for XGBoost using Optuna on a real dataset; report best ROC AUC
Use early stopping on a boosting model; observe how it picks n_estimators automatically
Compute and plot SHAP global feature importance vs sklearn's built-in importance for the same model; explain why they differ
weeks.project: Build a Kaggle-style Tabular Competition Solver. Pick a real competition (Titanic, House Prices, Tabular Playground Series). Build the full pipeline: EDA, feature engineering, three boosting models (XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost), stacking them with a logistic meta-learner. Target: top-25% on the public leaderboard. Document every decision in a NOTEBOOK.md so future-you can read it as a playbook.

weeks.title: Clustering and Dimensionality Reduction — When You Don't Have Labels
weeks.context: Most real-world data isn't labelled. Clustering finds structure. Dimensionality reduction makes high-dim data tractable and visualisable. This week you learn K-Means, DBSCAN, HDBSCAN, PCA, UMAP, t-SNE — and you learn when each lies to you.
topics: K-Means — the algorithm, elbow method, silhouette score, when k-means fails
DBSCAN and HDBSCAN — density-based clustering, no need to pre-specify k
Gaussian Mixture Models — soft clustering with probabilistic assignments
Hierarchical clustering — agglomerative, the dendrogram
PCA — when linear projection is enough
UMAP and t-SNE — non-linear embedding, visualisation only
Cluster evaluation — silhouette, Davies-Bouldin, when there are no labels
Anomaly detection — Isolation Forest, One-Class SVM, when these beat clustering
tasks: Cluster a customer dataset (e.g. Online Retail UCI) with K-Means; pick k via elbow + silhouette
Apply DBSCAN to the same data; compare clusters and what each picks up

Implement Isolation Forest for outlier detection on a known-anomaly dataset; measure AUC against ground-truth labels

weeks.project: Build a Customer Segmentation Tool. Take a real retail or e-commerce dataset (Kaggle Online Retail or RFM data). Compute RFM features per customer. Cluster with K-Means and HDBSCAN. Visualise with UMAP coloured by cluster. Profile each cluster (mean RFM, % of revenue, retention rate). Build a 1-page report a marketing team could act on. This is the kind of analysis that ships in real businesses every week.

weeks.title: Time Series — Forecasting When Order Matters
weeks.context: Time series breaks every standard ML assumption — your train/test split must respect time, your features must include history without leakage, your evaluation must be backtested. This week you learn the classical approaches (ARIMA, exponential smoothing) and the modern ones (gradient boosting on lag features, neural forecasters).
topics: Time series components — trend, seasonality, cyclicality, residual
Stationarity — what it is, how to test, how to achieve it
Classical models — ARIMA, SARIMA, exponential smoothing (ETS)
Feature engineering for time series — lags, rolling means, time features, calendar features
Cross-validation for time series — TimeSeriesSplit, walk-forward, why naive k-fold leaks
Forecasting metrics — MAPE, sMAPE, MASE; which to use when
Modern approaches — gradient boosting on engineered features, Prophet, neural forecasters
Multivariate and hierarchical forecasting — when you have related series
tasks: Forecast the Bike Sharing or Air Passengers dataset with three methods: ETS, SARIMA, gradient boosting on lag features
Compute sMAPE and MASE for each; compare on a held-out future window
Build proper walk-forward validation: predict day t+1 given data up to day t, slide forward, accumulate predictions
Apply Prophet to a dataset with strong seasonality; inspect the decomposed components
Demonstrate target leakage by including future information in your features; show how badly it overstates performance
weeks.project: Build a Sales Forecasting Tool. Pick a real retail or store dataset (M5 competition, Rossmann, or any local dataset). Build a per-SKU + per-store hierarchical forecasting pipeline: lag features, rolling stats, calendar effects (holidays in your region!), promotional flags. Model: LightGBM with target = sales. Walk-forward backtest over 6 months. Target: sMAPE under 25% on the test window. Compare to a naive seasonal baseline.
